title: Is that a knife?
hookLine: when someone asks about the kirpan, a calm short answer: an article of faith, kirpa and aan, mercy and honor

lines: AN AIRPORT. A SCHOOL. A NEW JOB.
cards: The airport security line. A school office on the first day of term. A new job, and a coworker who noticed a strap under a shirt.
Three places, one question, sometimes asked kindly, sometimes not: is that a knife? A week ago you met the kirpan as a duty to protect. Today, what to actually say when someone asks.

teach.b: Start with an answer that fits in one breath. Something like: it's a kirpan, an article of my faith; it stands for protecting people who can't protect themselves, and it's never used in anger.
Most people only need that much. If they want more, give them the name. Sikh teachers often explain kirpan as two words.

teach.h: KIRPA AND AAN — MERCY AND HONOR.
teach.b: Kirpa: grace, mercy, the word the Guru Granth Sahib uses again and again for God's kindness. And aan: honor, dignity.
Language scholars trace kirpan to an older Sanskrit word for a blade, so mercy and honor is a teaching reading rather than the root. But notice the order. Mercy comes first.
Then the practical part, said plainly. A kirpan is worn sheathed, on a cloth strap called a gatra, often small and under the clothes.

teach.h: RULES DIFFER FROM PLACE TO PLACE.
teach.b: Rules at airports, schools and workplaces differ from place to place. Airports in many countries allow no blade in the cabin, so Sikhs who fly plan ahead in different ways.

Courts in some countries have accepted the kirpan as a religious article with safeguards, like a sheath sewn shut. If you carry one, your gurdwara or a Sikh civil-rights group can tell you what applies where you live.
And if you don't carry one, the same short answer helps when someone asks you about a friend who does.

teach.h: HOW YOU ANSWER IS PART OF IT.
teach.b: Many Sikhs add one thing: how you answer is part of what the kirpan means. Calm, kind, unashamed.

how: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan at all times as one of the five Ks, sheathed on a cloth strap called a gatra and often under the clothes; when asked, many explain it briefly as an article of faith, often read as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor, and check the local rules for airports, schools and work.

practice: Think of a question people ask about who you are, or about someone you love: your name, your clothes, your faith, your family, and picture someone asking it, a little nervous, a little blunt.

Notice your first reaction, the tightening, breathe out through it, and find a calm answer in one sentence, in your own words, kind to them and true to you. Say it silently once, and picture them nodding.

wordCard.voice: The kirpan. An article of faith, often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor, and best explained the same way: calmly, mercy first.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirpa, grace or mercy; the first half of the common teaching reading of kirpan.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy first. In the answer, as much as in the sheath. Day two hundred seventy-six.
